title: Vision Correction
lead: Nearsightedness and farsightedness are the two most common defects of the eye, and each is corrected by a spectacle lens that makes an image the eye can see clearly. This section finds the power of the lens that corrects each defect, describes astigmatism and contact lenses, and explains how laser vision correction reshapes the cornea to change the power of the eye.
objectives: Identify and discuss common vision defects.
summary_html:
• Nearsightedness, or myopia, is the inability to see distant objects and is corrected with a diverging lens to reduce power.
  • Farsightedness, or hyperopia, is the inability to see close objects and is corrected with a converging lens to increase power.
  • In myopia and hyperopia, the corrective lenses produce images at a distance that the person can see clearly—the far point and near point, respectively.
notes: Ten of the module’s twenty problems have no keyed answer and are left out: the near point of eyes with an accommodated power of 53.5 D; the near point before a LASIK correction that adds 3.00 D; the correction for a far point of 5.00 cm; the distance examined by eyes of 53.0 D; the relaxed power and closest object of an administrator with a far point of 50.0 cm; the three problems that repeat an earlier one for glasses held 1.50 cm, 1.75 cm and 2.20 cm from the eyes; the nearsighted man shaving at a mirror; and the Unreasonable Results problem on a −4.00 D lens. The Integrated Concepts problem on the depth of cornea a LASIK burst ablates is printed in 26.6 and set here, where LASIK is taught; its temperatures, printed with an ordinal sign, are written in °C. References to Geometric Optics are plain text.

Ten of the twenty problems have no keyed answer and are left out, and they are named in the section’s notes; where a keyed problem asks for a discussion as its last part, the book’s words for that part are in the solution. figures.original_caption: (Figure 26.5) (a) The nearsighted (myopic) eye converges rays from a distant object in front of the retina; thus, they are diverging when they strike the retina, producing a blurry image. This can be caused by the lens of the eye being too powerful or the length of the eye being too great. (b) The farsighted (hyperopic) eye is unable to converge the rays from a close object by the time they strike the retina, producing blurry close vision. This can be caused by insufficient power in the lens or by the eye being too short. (Figure 26.6) Correction of nearsightedness requires a diverging lens that compensates for the overconvergence by the eye. The diverging lens produces an image closer to the eye than the object, so that the nearsighted person can see it clearly. (Figure 26.7) Correction of farsightedness uses a converging lens that compensates for the under convergence by the eye. The converging lens produces an image farther from the eye than the object, so that the farsighted person can see it clearly.

This chart can detect astigmatism, unevenness in the focus of the eye. Check each of your eyes separately by looking at the center cross (without spectacles if you wear them). If lines along some axes appear darker or clearer than others, you have an astigmatism.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following types of light have a wavelength greater than that of visible light? (I) gamma rays, (II) infrared, (III) radio, (IV) ultraviolet.

answer.hint: Recall the order of the electromagnetic spectrum from Chapter 24: wavelength grows from gamma rays through ultraviolet, visible light and infrared to radio waves.

exercises.prompt: In LASIK surgery, a coherent UV light of 193 nm is focused on the corneal tissue. (a) Explain the importance of using light that is all the same wavelength. (b) Explain why UV light is more effective than infrared light at evaporating the corneal tissue.

answer.solution: (a) Light of one wavelength can be focused to a small, well-defined spot, since a lens bends every part of it by the same amount, and all of it is absorbed in the same way by the cornea. The depth of tissue each burst removes is then predictable, which is what lets the surgeon control the reshaping precisely. (b) Ultraviolet light has a higher frequency than infrared light, so each photon carries more energy, and the 193 nm light is very strongly absorbed in a thin surface layer of the cornea. Its energy is deposited in a very thin layer that is evaporated, rather than spread more deeply through the tissue as heat.

exercises.prompt: It has become common to replace the cataract-clouded lens of the eye with an internal lens. This intraocular lens can be chosen so that the person has perfect distant vision. Will the person be able to read without glasses? If the person was nearsighted, is the power of the intraocular lens greater or less than the removed lens?

answer.solution: No. The intraocular lens has a fixed power and cannot accommodate, so an eye set for perfect distant vision cannot add the power needed for close vision, and the person will need reading glasses. A nearsighted eye had too much power, so to give perfect distant vision the intraocular lens is chosen with less power than the lens it replaces.

exercises.prompt: If the cornea is to be reshaped (this can be done surgically or with contact lenses) to correct myopia, should its curvature be made greater or smaller? Explain. Also explain how hyperopia can be corrected.

answer.solution: A myopic eye has too much power, and the cornea supplies about two-thirds of that power, so its curvature should be made smaller: a flatter cornea bends rays less and lowers the power of the eye. Hyperopia is the opposite, an eye with too little power, so it is corrected by making the curvature of the cornea greater, which raises the power of the eye.

exercises.prompt: If there is a fixed percent uncertainty in LASIK reshaping of the cornea, why would you expect those people with the greatest correction to have a poorer chance of normal distant vision after the procedure?

answer.solution: A fixed percent uncertainty is a larger uncertainty in diopters when the correction is larger. For example, 5% of a 2.00 D correction is 0.10 D, which the eye hardly notices, while 5% of a 10.0 D correction is 0.50 D, enough to leave distant vision blurred. People who need the greatest correction are therefore the most likely to be left with a noticeable error.

exercises.prompt: A person with presbyopia has lost some or all of the ability to accommodate the power of the eye. If such a person’s distant vision is corrected with LASIK, will she still need reading glasses? Explain.

answer.solution: Yes. LASIK changes the fixed power of the cornea so that the relaxed eye focuses distant objects on the retina, but it does not restore the lens’s ability to increase its power for close objects. Since presbyopia is the loss of that ability, she still cannot add the power needed for close vision, and a converging reading lens must supply it.

exercises.prompt: What is the far point of a person whose eyes have a relaxed power of 50.5 D?

answer.hint: The relaxed eye focuses its far point on the retina, so use $P = 1/\kdobj + 1/\kdimg$ with $\kdimg = 0.0200$ m and solve for $\kdobj$.

exercises.prompt: (a) A laser vision correction reshaping the cornea of a myopic patient reduces the power of his eye by 9.00 D, with a $\pm 5.0\%$ uncertainty in the final correction. What is the range of diopters for spectacle lenses that this person might need after LASIK procedure? (b) Was the person nearsighted or farsighted before the procedure? How do you know?

parts.part: (a) the size of the range either side of zero, ±
parts.hint: The uncertainty is 5.0% of the 9.00 D correction, and a spectacle lens would have to make up for it.

answer.solution: (a) $\pm 0.45\ \text{D}$ (b) The person was nearsighted because the patient was myopic and the power was reduced.

exercises.prompt: What was the previous far point of a patient who had laser vision correction that reduced the power of her eye by 7.00 D, producing normal distant vision for her?

answer.hint: Before the correction her relaxed eye had 7.00 D more than the 50.0 D that focuses a distant object, and that extra power is $1/\kdobj$ for her far point.

exercises.prompt: A student’s eyes, while reading the blackboard, have a power of 51.0 D. How far is the board from his eyes?
A young woman with normal distant vision has a 10.0% ability to accommodate (that is, increase) the power of her eyes. What is the closest object she can see clearly?

answer.hint: Her relaxed power is 50.0 D, so her greatest power is 10.0% more; the extra power is $1/\kdobj$ for her near point.

exercises.prompt: A very myopic man has a far point of 20.0 cm. What power contact lens (when on the eye) will correct his distant vision?

answer.hint: A contact lens sits on the eye, so it must make an image of a distant object 20.0 cm in front of it: $\kdobj = \infty$ and $\kdimg = -0.200$ m.

exercises.prompt: A myopic person sees that their contact lens prescription is $-4.00\ \text{D}$. What is their far point?

answer.hint: The lens makes an image of a distant object at the far point, so $P = 1/\infty + 1/\kdimg$; the far point is the distance $|\kdimg|$.

exercises.prompt: The contact lens prescription for a mildly farsighted person is 0.750 D, and the person has a near point of 29.0 cm. What is the power of the tear layer between the cornea and the lens if the correction is ideal, taking the tear layer into account?

answer.hint: Find the power that makes an image of an object 25.0 cm away at 29.0 cm on the same side; the contact lens and the tear layer together supply it, and their powers add.

exercises.prompt: A teacher sees that a child’s contact lens prescription is 0.750 D. What is the child’s near point?

answer.hint: The contact lens takes an object at 25.0 cm and makes an image at the near point: $P = 1/0.250\ \text{m} + 1/\kdimg$, and the near point is $|\kdimg|$.

exercises.prompt: The contact lens prescription for a nearsighted person is $-4.00\ \text{D}$ and the person has a far point of 22.5 cm. What is the power of the tear layer between the cornea and the lens if the correction is ideal, taking the tear layer into account?

answer.hint: The ideal correction makes an image of a distant object at 22.5 cm, which takes $-1/0.225\ \text{m}$; the contact lens and the tear layer together supply it, and their powers add.

exercises.prompt: Integrated Concepts (a) During laser vision correction, a brief burst of 193 nm ultraviolet light is projected onto the cornea of the patient. It makes a spot 1.00 mm in diameter and deposits 0.500 mJ of energy. Calculate the depth of the layer ablated, assuming the corneal tissue has the same properties as water and is initially at 34.0°C. The tissue’s temperature is increased to 100°C and evaporated without further temperature increase. (b) Does your answer imply that the shape of the cornea can be finely controlled?

parts.part: (a) the depth of the layer ablated
parts.hint: The energy heats a mass $m$ of water from 34.0°C to 100°C and then evaporates it, $Q = mc\Delta T + mL_{\text{v}}$; the mass is the density times the area of the spot times the depth.

answer.solution: (a) $0.251\ \mu\text{m}$ (b) Yes, this thickness implies that the shape of the cornea can be very finely controlled, producing normal distant vision in more than 90% of patients.
